pages.translation: ...if a hot air makes the minds of men sharper: but it cools [them] and [makes them] slower. Since, however, the median nations are of the sharpest minds and the highest skill of [their] generations, they are for fortitude and magnanimity. I have said that the itinerary of the minds from the sun erupts from these. Those which refrigerate, are born in regions prepared for the vehemence of arms, in great, invincible [acts], without fear; but with slowness of mind, they rush without resistance. Without skill, they resist by their own counsels. Since, therefore, [mankind] is set among the things in the world and all nations are set in moderate mixtures: since, indeed, it possesses the space of the whole orb of the earth and the region in the middle of the world by the reason of things. Therefore, it stands most temperately toward both sides of the body and, indeed, in strengths, it is the most brave of nations. Just as the star of Mars in the heavens is very hot, and [Saturn] is very cold, the middle [planet] creates a temperate [state], by the same reason Italy, between the northern and the Indian [nations], by mixtures tempered from both sides, holds invincible [lands], and cools the itineraries of the barbarians by its counsel, and the thoughts of the Indians by a strong hand and by counsels. Thus, the divine mind placed the city of the Roman people in an excellent and temperate region, so that it might rule the orb of the earth. Since nature has created different regions by the inclinations of the sky for various generations, [and] since the nature of the spirits of the generations [is] distinct, the quality of the things which are born; I do not doubt that I should distribute the reasons of the buildings aptly to the nation and to the quality of the generations. I await from the skill of the things themselves to show [this]. Since I have set forth the reasons for the supreme power of the places, disposed by the nature of things; but how it is fitting to construct the reasons of the buildings to the inclinations of the sky for the generations, and [I] have described the nature of the figures in buildings, the limetars [and] the smaller separations, I will explain. No care should be greater for the architect than that the buildings should have the exactness of reason in proportions. Since, therefore, the reason of symmetry was set in the explanation of the arrangements: since, indeed, it [is] sharp: it is not shameful to add to the symmetry, either for use or for beauty, by additions, [and] by tempering. [If] it is said concerning symmetry that it is taken away or added, so that it is indicated that it was formed correctly; in appearance, nothing is missing. Another thing seems not to be in the appearance of the hand; another in a high place; not the same in an enclosure; [it is] different in the open, in which the works of great sapience are to be done at length. The sight does not seem to have the effect of sight; but it is often deceived in judgment by that which is placed, just as those things which are seen on the stage, the projection of columns, the figures of the signs of the spheres of the mechanics, [and] the projections, if they are placed without doubt to the plane rule. Similarly, in ships, the oars, if they are directed under the water, they are called broken; when they are directed, although they touch the surface of the water, they appear straight between them. When they are lowered under the water, by the transparency of the light, the image flowing from their bodies is sent back to the surface of the water; and these, by ignorance, are caused to be seen as a broken oar-blade. These, however, whether by the impulse of a simulacrum or by the outpourings of rays, as the physicists please, we see that the reason is such that the judgments of the eyes have a false aspect. Since, therefore, those things which are seen as false, but are not [false], but are presented to the eyes otherwise, it is necessary to make additions or subtractions according to the necessity or the place, so that nothing is missing from these works. This, however, is not explained by the ignorance of the masters; but when the length of the space of the place is built, the magnitude is [set] once. It follows that the proportioning to the beauty is made ready, so that [the things] will be clear to those sitting. After a hundred and one *yojanas*, he touched his crown and returned; with a single thought, he saw the Samantabhadra master.
Majestic, he is present on the red lotus seat;
Clearly, he is the white elephant child.
When the wisdom and compassion of the sand-kalpas are full,
When the vows and practices of the minute particles are perfect,
The Buddha's ocean of virtue is proclaimed again;
I worry to see the waves churning and vast. <gloss>Foguo Bai</gloss>

Beating the drum and playing the *pipa* <note>a four-stringed plucked lute</note>, he returns to his own assembly.
The wooden boy can clap his hands; the stone woman knows how to boil tea.
Clouds scatter, the moon appears at the edge of the sky; spring comes, flowers bloom on the trees.
Sudhana has visited everywhere; the black beans have not yet sprouted. <gloss>Yanqing Zhong</gloss>

<margin>Added sequel</margin> Sudhana traveled through one hundred and ten cities, visiting fifty-three good teachers. Finally, he arrived in front of the Vairochana Tower. The previous day was the place where one dwells in the emptiness, the signless, and the effortless <note>terms for the realization of non-attachment</note>. He saw the tower gate closed. Sudhana, for a moment, gathered his thoughts and said, "With great compassion, I pray that the tower gate opens and lets me enter." Maitreya, leading his retinue, arrived before Sudhana. With a snap of his fingers, the tower gate opened. Sudhana entered. Once inside, the gate closed again. He saw hundreds of thousands of billions of towers; in each tower, there was a Maitreya leading a retinue, and a Sudhana standing face to face before them. Maitreya snapped his fingers again and said, "Good man, arise. The nature of Dharma is like this."

A Verse says:

The wondrous intention of the child is collected at the very end.
Sudhana stops his southern journey here.
Suddenly he enters the Vairochana Treasury;
He regrets having gone to other mountains to see monks. <gloss>Zhang Wujin</gloss>

On the lone peak of Mount Miaofeng, there is no teacher.
Traveling to one hundred and ten cities was a waste for Sudhana.
If the tower were revealed by a snap of the fingers,
Clearly, one has eyes but has never opened them. <gloss>Huotian Ti</gloss>

Fifty-three people, strung on a single thread.
Though the child is small, his courage is like the sky.
Vast is the misty water, without number;
Buying the scenery costs no money at all. <gloss>Beijian Jian</gloss>

<summary>The page concludes Sudhana's journey at the Vairochana Tower, illustrating the realization of the non-dual, infinite nature of reality through Maitreya's guidance.</summary>
<keywords>Sudhana, Maitreya, Vairochana Tower, Non-duality, Chan realization</keywords>

...water, until today shining long in the slanting evening sun. <gloss>Guyun Quan</gloss>
Three inches from the hook, a shackle; one oar, and hundreds of thousands of pores feel a cold chill. Although both hands personally entrust it, it requires that fellow to nod his head himself. <gloss>Wujin Pai</gloss>
Jiashan in those years misused his mind. Greedy for the scented bait, he was captured by him. Nodding three times without a word; the water is wide, the mountains are distant, the resentment grows deeper. <gloss>Zheweng Yan</gloss>
With no place the size of an awl to contain his body, he instead drifts in a lone boat, occupying the crucial ferry. Not only did Jiashan suffer the poisonous hand, until today he has tricked to death a boatload of people. <gloss>Xiaoweng Kan</gloss>
Matching words to respond to the boatman is just like digging in the ground to seek the blue sky. Even if the oar were to thoroughly illuminate, it is still a leaky boat in Huating. <gloss>Sutai Bian</gloss>
No appearance and no flaw, then surrender. It is only because he lightly believed the wise wandering monk. If he had not arrived at Huating, what could the iron-cast boat oar do to you? <gloss>Nansou Jian</gloss>
In the depths of the Zhu River, a flat boat drifts. The clever wandering monk holds the straight hook. One oar to the mouth empties the universe. The distant mountains are layered, and the water is serene. <gloss>Gelu Tan</gloss>
In the laughter, he abandoned the Bamboo Grove Temple, thinking that Huating had much to offer. Exhausting life under the oar; thinking carefully, success and failure are just like Xiao He <note>a reference to the Han dynasty figure, implying fickle fortunes</note>. <gloss>Mozong Ben</gloss>
More than thirty years at Yaoshan, how could the life-activities of the ghost family be transmitted? At that time, if you had not obtained old Jiashan, you would just have to be patient and pole a broken boat. <gloss>Qingxi Che</gloss>

<column-break/>

Chuanzi instructed Jiashan, "From here on, you must go to a place where you hide your body and leave no traces. In the place where there are no traces, do not hide your body. I spent twenty years at Yaoshan only to clarify this matter. Now that you have obtained it, later do not reside in cities or crowded villages. Just go into the deep mountains and take a mattock <note>a digging tool, symbolizing a reclusive life of labor</note>..."

<summary>Further poetic reflections on the transmission between Chuanzi and Jiashan, followed by Chuanzi's final instructions to his successor.</summary>

# Deshan

<meta>The text discusses the encounter between the monk Luopu, his master Linji, and the master Deshan.</meta>

Luopu followed the instructions and asked. The master immediately struck. Luopu caught the staff and gave it a push. The master then returned to the abbot's quarters. Luopu returned and reported this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. However, do you recognize Deshan?" Luopu hesitated, and Linji struck him.
<gloss>Added note</gloss>
The Xiongnu warrior prides himself on his skills, thinking he surpasses others. The young general goes to give orders. When he actually reaches the enemy, he wins a small battle, but upon returning, he cannot save his whole body <note>a metaphor for losing one's essence through arrogance</note>.
<gloss>Haiyin Xin</gloss>
<gloss>Fojian Qin</gloss>
Like a parrot in a golden cage, its back is like red jade, a green-clad servant. Although it has learned human speech, when you ask it something, it actually knows nothing at all.

<column-break/>

Deshan had a monk come to pay respects, and he shut the door. The monk knocked on the door. The master asked, "Who is it?" He replied, "A lion." The master opened the door. The monk circled in and bowed. The master jumped on his head and rode him, saying, "You animal, where have you been for so long?"
Verse:
<gloss>Added note</gloss>
Seeing a rabbit, one releases the hawk; by means of the false, one strikes the true. Before your feet have crossed the threshold, you must awaken suddenly.
<gloss>Mu'an Yong</gloss>
Deshan ascended the hall and said, "The great assembly knows it all. Even if the Buddhas of the three periods had their mouths hung on the wall, there would still be one person laughing loudly. If you recognize this person, your studies are complete."
<gloss>Or written as the secret words of Yuanming</gloss>
Touzi Qingyun said: Even so, the great companions of Deshan have hidden everything. The moon in the Chu sky still contains the stars of the Han land. He composed a verse:
The two blind men enter the dark, the road is rugged. The sun sets, the reeds provide a moment's rest. How can it compare to the stone man sleeping at midnight, avoiding the need for the emperor to guard the forest retreat? You must know that the blossoming of flowers is not related to the wood. When the legless one walks, he has already touched the path. Yesterday the wind rose on the Chang'an road; originally it was a map of the Kunlun frontier. I hold the throat, the wind grinds the clouds, the water is cold, the sky is autumn. Do not say the colorful scales have no flavor; he fished out the moon of the Canglang with one cast.
<note>Tiandong Jue</note>

<summary>This page presents dialogues regarding Deshan's aggressive teaching methods and metaphors for enlightenment.</summary>

**Recorded Sayings of the Ancestral Masters**
Eighth generation after the Sixth Patriarch; seventh generation after Nanyang [Huizhong].

Chan Master Shouchu of Dongshan in Xiangzhou, a dharma heir of Yunmen. 
When he first visited Yunmen, the master asked, "Where did you just come from?"
The master replied, "Xixia."
[Yunmen] asked, "Where were you during the summer?"
The master replied, "Hunan."
[Yunmen] asked, "When did you leave Hunan?"
The master replied, "In the autumn."
[Yunmen] said, "I give you thirty blows."

The master asked, "What was my fault?"
[Yunmen] replied, "Jiangxi and Hunan, just like that."
At these words, the master was suddenly enlightened.

I have read in the *History of the Han Dynasty* <note>original: "Han Chuan"</note> how Sima Changqing <note>Sima Xiangru, a famous poet</note> returned to his home in Chengdu to find only four bare walls standing. I have also seen in the Tang Dynasty calligraphy rubbings how Yan Lugong <note>Yan Zhenqing, a noted official and calligrapher</note> begged for rice from Lord Li. Alas! Even figures of the Han and Tang like Changqing and Lugong, who could be called grand, eminent, and heroic, still had broken houses and insufficient gruel. How much more so for those of lesser status! Yet the lingering excellence of these two men’s characters can still be imagined. As for my own unworthiness, my reputation is dull and forgotten, and I have sunk to the bottom. This is because the gap between wisdom and folly cannot be shifted, and the distance between the noble and the lowly is vast; there is no use in envying them. However, I still find something to envy in Changqing and Lugong: I envy that they were alone in their plight. Changqing was indeed weary of travel when he returned, and his only burden was his wife, Wenjun; he still had those "four walls" to boast of. But in my case, I have sought a government salary and not yet attained it, while my parents are now both old and I have no means to support them. My younger brothers and sisters are numerous, reaching the age for marriage—more than twenty mouths in total. All these responsibilities are

I once visited Ma-ren Temple with Lin Min-gong and Zi-ren. Although it was known for its adherence to the <term>Vinaya</term> <gloss>monastic rules</gloss>, its Chan regulations were no less strict than elsewhere. The granaries had no surplus grain. He was seventy-eight years old and had been a monk for fifty-two years. On the day of his <term>cremation</term> <gloss>ritual burning</gloss>, the flames turned five colors and a white light leaped upward. Wherever the smoke reached, <term>sarira</term> <gloss>sacred relics</gloss> were distributed. Over a thousand people, both monastics and laity, obtained them, and those remaining were beyond counting. A stupa was built for him at the foot of <term>Duxiu Feng</term> <gloss>Solitary Beauty Peak</gloss>. 

The Master was pure, sincere, and compassionate by nature. His refined spirit was extraordinary and elegantly transcendent. He treated everyone, whether strangers or kin, noble or humble, with a warm face and soft words, showing equal respect to all. He presided over the <term>Conglin</term> <gloss>monastic community</gloss> with very strict discipline; those who violated orders were certainly punished without pardon. For this reason, the five seats of the practice centers he held became models for all directions. He attained the <term>Samadhi of Playful Joy</term> and possessed the eloquence of joyful preaching. His sharp wit and wisdom cut down the forest of heterodoxy like falling clouds or collapsing rocks. He opened up the Right View, which shone as clearly as the sun in a blue sky. Everyone felt they had reached the profound depths. However, when entering his room for private instruction, he was like a bronze cliff or an iron wall, impossible to scale.

<summary>The miraculous events of Master Zhenjing's cremation and a description of his dual character: compassionate and polite in person, yet strict in discipline and profound in teaching.</summary>

A commoner from Shuzhou named Ke Meng encountered an extraordinary monk at the foot of Mount Sui. The monk pointed his staff at a pine root and told Meng to carve into it. ...you do not know that the body is fundamentally the same as emptiness. The body and the shadow are fundamentally no different. Do not have one existence or one non-existence. If you want to keep one and discard the other, you will forever be distant from the true principle. If you further love the sage and hate the ordinary, you will drift and sink in the sea of birth and death. Afflictions exist because of the mind; if there is no mind, where would the afflictions dwell? Do not labor to differentiate or grasp and discard; naturally, you will attain the Dao in an instant. When dreaming, one creates things in the dream; when awake, there is absolutely nothing. The thinking while awake and the dream are inverted; the two views are not different. To change from confusion to awakening and seek profit is no different from a peddling merchant. When movement and stillness are both forgotten, constant silence naturally accords with true suchness. If one says that sentient beings are different from the Buddha, it is far and eternally distinct from the Buddha. The Buddha and sentient beings are not two; it is naturally complete without remainder.

The nature of Dharma is fundamentally always silent, vast, and without boundaries. If the mind grasps between grasping and discarding, it is replaced by that one state. Restrain your appearance, enter <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditation</gloss>, sit in Zen, control your environment, and settle your mind. If you carefully examine the mechanism, it is like a wooden person. How can one ever reach the other shore in cultivating the Dao? All phenomena are fundamentally empty, and there is no true attachment.

We only discuss seeing one's true nature <note>original: "見性", the core realization in Zen</note>. We do not discuss meditative concentration <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> or liberation. 

Yinzong asked: Why do you not discuss meditative concentration and liberation? 

Huineng replied: Because these are two separate things, and thus not the Buddha-Dharma. The Buddha-Dharma is a teaching of non-duality <note>original: "不二之法", the principle that reality is not composed of opposing pairs</note>. 

Yinzong asked again: What is this Buddha-Dharma of non-duality? 

Huineng said: Master, you lecture on the Nirvana Sutra. This sutra clarifies that seeing the Buddha-nature is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality. As the Nirvana Sutra states, the Bodhisattva Noble Virtue King asked the Buddha: If someone commits the four gravest sins, the five heinous crimes, or is an <term>icchantika</term> <gloss>one who lacks the seeds of enlightenment</gloss>, do they cut off their roots of goodness and their Buddha-nature? 

The Buddha replied: There are two kinds of roots of goodness. The first is permanent, and the second is impermanent. However, the Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent. Therefore, it is never cut off. This is called non-duality. Furthermore, there is good and there is not-good. The Buddha-nature is neither good nor not-good. This is called non-duality. Ordinary people see the physical aggregates and the sensory realms as two separate things. The wise realize that their nature is not two. This nature of non-duality is the Buddha-nature.

Upon hearing this, Yinzong rejoiced and joined his palms in reverence. He said: My lecturing on the sutras is like common rubble, while your discussion of the meaning is like pure gold. 

Thereupon, he shaved Huineng’s head and requested to serve him as a disciple. Huineng then opened the Dharma Gate of the East Mountain <note>the lineage of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren</note> under a Bodhi tree. 

Huineng continued: I received the Dharma at East Mountain and endured extreme hardships. My life hung by a thread. That I am able to meet with the Prefect, the officials, monks, nuns, and laypeople in this assembly today is due to causes from many kalpas <gloss>eons</gloss> ago. It is also because you made offerings to many Buddhas in past lives and planted shared roots of goodness that you are now able to hear this sudden teaching <note>original: "頓教", the doctrine of immediate enlightenment</note> and the causes of my receiving the Dharma. This teaching was passed down by the ancient sages; it is not my own personal wisdom. Those who wish to hear the teaching of the ancient sages should each purify their minds. After hearing it, each of you will resolve your own doubts, becoming no different from the sages of past generations.

The Master then addressed the assembly: Good friends, the wisdom of <term>Bodhi-Prajna</term> <gloss>enlightened wisdom</gloss> is something people of this world inherently possess. It is only because the mind is deluded that they cannot realize it themselves. They must rely on a great spiritual friend to show them the way and guide them to see their nature. You should know that there is no difference in the Buddha-nature of an ignorant person and a wise person. It is only because of the difference between delusion and awakening that some are ignorant and some are wise. I shall now speak to you of the Great <term>Prajna Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> so that each of you may attain wisdom. Listen carefully with a sincere heart, and I will speak for you.

Good friends, people of the world recite <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> with their mouths all day long, but they do not recognize the <term>Prajna</term> of their own nature. This is like talking about food but never becoming full. If you only speak of emptiness with your mouth, you will not see your nature even after ten thousand kalpas. In the end, there is no benefit. 

Good friends, <term>Maha Prajna Paramita</term> is a Sanskrit term. In our language, it means "Great Wisdom that reaches the Other Shore." This must be practiced in the heart; it does not consist of oral recitation. If the mouth recites it but the heart does not practice it, it is of no use.

<summary>Huineng explains the principle of non-duality through the Nirvana Sutra and begins his public teaching on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, emphasizing internal practice over mere recitation.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Yinzong, non-duality, Buddha-nature, Nirvana Sutra, Prajna Paramita, sudden teaching, East Mountain Dharma Gate</keywords>

多。迷人不能省覺。念念起惡。常行惡道。迴一念善。智慧即生。此名自性化身佛。何名圓滿報身。譬如一燈能除千年暗。一智能滅萬年愚。莫思向前。已過不可得。常思於後。念念圓明。自見本性。善惡雖殊。本性無二。無二之性。名為實性。於實性中。不染善惡。此名圓滿報身。自性起一念惡。滅萬劫善因。自性起一念善。得恆沙惡盡。直至無上菩提。念念自見。不失本念。名為報身。善知識。從法身思量。即是化身佛。念念自性自見。即是報身佛。自悟自修自性功德。是真歸依。皮肉是色身。色身是舍宅。不言歸依也。但悟自性三身。即識自性佛。吾有一無相頌。若能誦持。言下令汝積劫迷罪一時消滅。頌曰。迷人修福不修道。只言修福便是道。布施供養福無邊。心中三惡元來造。擬將修福欲滅罪。後世得福罪還在。但向心中除罪緣。各自性中真懺悔。忽悟大乘真懺悔。除邪行正即無罪。學道常於自性觀。即與諸佛同一類。吾祖惟傳此頓法。普願見性同一體。若欲當來覓法身。離諸法相心中洗。努力自見莫悠悠。後念忽絕一世休。若悟大乘得見性。虔恭合掌至心求。師言。善知識。總須誦取。依此修行。言下見性。雖去吾千里。如常在吾邊。於此言下不悟。即對面千里。何勤遠來。珍重好去。一眾聞法。靡不開悟。歡喜奉行。

There are many such people. Deluded people cannot awaken themselves. Their every thought gives rise to evil, and they constantly walk the paths of evil. Yet, if they turn back a single thought toward goodness, wisdom is immediately born. This is called the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Transformation Body</gloss> of one's own nature.

What is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Reward Body</gloss>? Just as a single lamp can dispel a thousand years of darkness, a single flash of wisdom can extinguish ten thousand years of ignorance. Do not dwell on what came before; the past is gone and cannot be recovered. Always think of what comes after. Let every thought be perfect and bright, and you will see your own original nature. Although good and evil differ, the original nature is not two. This non-dual nature is called the true nature. Within this true nature, one is not stained by either good or evil. This is called the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Reward Body</gloss>.

If a single evil thought arises from one's own nature, it destroys the good causes of ten thousand <term>kalpas</term> <gloss>aeons</gloss>. If a single good thought arises from one's own nature, it ends evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, leading directly to supreme <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Enlightenment</gloss>. To see for oneself in every thought and never lose the original thought is called the Reward Body.

Learned friends, to deliberate from the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> is the Transformation Body Buddha. When every thought sees into its own nature, that is the Reward Body Buddha. To realize and cultivate the merit of one's own nature for oneself is the true refuge. The skin and flesh are the physical body; the physical body is merely a house and is not spoken of as a refuge. Simply realize the three bodies of your own nature, and you will recognize the Buddha of your own nature.

I have a Verse of Formlessness. If you can recite and maintain it, it will cause the deluded sins accumulated over many aeons to vanish the moment the words are spoken. The verse says:

Deluded people cultivate blessings but not the Way,
Claiming that cultivating blessings is the Way itself.
While the blessings from charity and offerings are limitless,
The three evils remain rooted in the mind.
By attempting to use the cultivation of blessings to wipe out sins,
One receives blessings in future lives, but the sins remain.
One must simply remove the conditions of sin from within the mind,
And practice true repentance within one's own nature.
A sudden realization of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> true repentance,
Removing the false and practicing the right, leaves one without sin.
Those who study the Way should constantly observe their own nature;
They are then of the same kind as all Buddhas.
Our ancestors transmitted only this sudden teaching,
Wishing that all might see their nature and become one substance.
If you wish to seek the Truth Body in the future,
Leave all appearances of phenomena and wash your heart within.
Strive to see it for yourself; do not drift aimlessly.
If the next thought is suddenly cut off, this life is over.
If you realize the Great Vehicle and see your nature,
Join your palms in reverence and seek it with a sincere heart.

The Master said: Learned friends, you must all recite this and practice according to it. If you see your nature upon hearing these words, then even if you are a thousand miles from me, it will be as if you are always by my side. If you do not realize it upon hearing these words, then even if we are face to face, we are a thousand miles apart. Why bother coming from so far? Take care and go well.

The entire assembly heard the Dharma, and there were none who did not achieve awakening. They rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

<summary>The Sixth Patriarch explains the Reward Body of Buddha and provides the Verse of Formlessness to guide practitioners in seeing their true nature rather than merely seeking external blessings. He emphasizes that true repentance and sudden enlightenment come from within the mind.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Platform Sutra, Reward Body, Transformation Body, Verse of Formlessness, Repentance, Buddha-nature, Sudden Enlightenment</keywords>

A person who is thoroughly realized has no sense of grasping or rejecting. By knowing the <term>five skandhas</term> <gloss>the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness</gloss> and the self within those aggregates, they see that all external forms and every sound are equal, like a dream or an illusion. They do not give rise to views of "ordinary" or "holy," nor do they form intellectual interpretations of <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state of liberation from suffering and rebirth</gloss>. The two extremes <note>such as existence and non-existence</note> and the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note> are cut off. They constantly respond to the functions of the sensory organs, yet they do not give rise to the thought of "functioning." They distinguish all phenomena, yet do not give rise to the thought of "distinction." Even when the fires at the end of an eon burn the seabed, or the winds lash the mountains against one another, the joy of true, eternal, and peaceful extinction remains. Such is the nature of Nirvana. I now speak of it under constraint to make you abandon false views. Do not follow my words with literal interpretations, and I will allow that you have understood a small portion. Zhidao heard this verse and attained great awakening. Overjoyed, he bowed and withdrew.

Zen Master Xingsi was born to the Liu family in Ancheng, Jizhou. Hearing that the Dharma seat at Caoxi was flourishing, he went directly to pay his respects. He asked, "What must one do so as not to fall into stages or ranks?" The Master <note>Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch</note> asked, "What have you been doing?" Xingsi replied, "I do not even practice the Holy Truths." The Master asked, "Then what stage have you fallen into?" Xingsi replied, "If I do not even practice the Holy Truths, what stage could there be?" The Master deeply appreciated his capacity and made Xingsi the leader of the assembly. One day, the Master told him, "You should go and teach in your own region so that the lineage is not cut off." Having received the Dharma, Xingsi returned to Mount Qingyuan in Jizhou to spread the teachings. He was posthumously titled Zen Master Hongji.

Zen Master Huairang was the son of the Du family in Jinzhou. He first visited National Teacher Anguo at Mount Song. Anguo sent him to Caoxi to consult the Master. When Huairang arrived and bowed, the Master asked, "Where do you come from?" Huairang replied, "From Mount Song." The Master asked, "What is this thing that has come here?" Huairang replied, "To say it is like a thing would be off the mark." The Master asked, "Can it still be cultivated and realized?" Huairang replied, "It is not that there is no cultivation or realization, but it cannot be defiled." The Master said, "Just this 'not being defiled' is what all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. You are like this, and I am like this too. Prajnatara of India predicted that a young horse would emerge from under your feet and trample the people of the world. This will happen in your heart; there is no need to speak of it quickly." Huairang suddenly understood. He served the Master for fifteen years, growing deeper in the profound mysteries every day. Later, he went to Nanyue and greatly promoted the Zen school.

Zen Master Xuanjue of Yongjia studied the sutras and commentaries in his youth and was an expert in the Tiantai school's <term>Samatha-Vipasyana</term> <gloss>calm abiding and insight</gloss> methods. While reading the Vimalakirti Sutra, he realized the ground of his mind. By chance, the Master's disciple Xuance visited him and had a deep discussion. Xuanjue's words were in secret agreement with the Patriarchs. Xuance asked, "Who was your teacher when you attained the Dharma?" Xuanjue said, "I listened to the <term>Vaipulya</term> <gloss>extensive or Mahayana</gloss> sutras and commentaries, and each had a teacher. Later, I realized the Buddha-mind school through the Vimalakirti Sutra, but I have no one to verify it." Xuance said, "Before the time of the King of Awesome Sound <note>the first Buddha of the remote past</note>, that would have been fine."

<summary>This page records the Sixth Patriarch Huineng's instructions on the nature of Nirvana and his initial encounters with three major disciples: Xingsi, Huairang, and Xuanjue. These meetings emphasize direct realization over intellectual study and formal stages of practice.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Xingsi, Huairang, Xuanjue, Nirvana, Vimalakirti Sutra, Zen lineage, Mount Qingyuan, Nanyue, Caoxi</keywords>

And thus they are established. All things are the original mind producing ten thousand kinds of phenomena. Therefore, the sutra says: when the mind arises, various phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease. If you wish to achieve the <term>All-Knowledge</term> <gloss>the wisdom of a Buddha</gloss>, you must attain the <term>Samadhi of One Appearance</term> <gloss>a state of meditative concentration on the non-duality of all things</gloss> and the <term>Samadhi of One Practice</term> <gloss>the constant practice of maintaining a straightforward mind</gloss>. If, in all places, you do not cling to appearances, and within those appearances you do not give rise to resentment or love, nor have any grasping or rejection, and do not dwell on matters of profit, loss, or destruction, but remain peaceful, quiet, empty, harmonious, and indifferent, this is called the Samadhi of One Appearance. If, in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you maintain a pure and straightforward mind, without moving from the <term>Bodhimaṇḍa</term> <gloss>place of enlightenment</gloss>, truly becoming the Pure Land, this is called the Samadhi of One Practice. If a person possesses these two samadhis, it is like the earth having seeds: they are contained, nourished, and their fruits are matured. The Samadhi of One Appearance and One Practice are just like this. My current teaching of the Law is like a timely rain, universally moistening the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like the seeds; meeting this moisture, they all begin to grow. Those who receive my instructions will certainly attain <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Those who follow my practice will surely realize the wonderful fruit. Listen to my verse:

The mind-ground contains all seeds,
Under the universal rain, all sprout.
Once the flower of sudden enlightenment is realized,
The fruit of Bodhi naturally matures.

After the Master spoke the verse, he said: The Law is not dual, and the mind is the same. The Way is pure and without any appearances. You must be careful not to contemplate stillness or empty your minds. This mind is originally pure; there is nothing to grasp or reject. Each of you must exert yourselves and go well according to circumstances. At that time, the disciples bowed and withdrew.

On the eighth day of the seventh month, the Grand Master suddenly said to his followers: I wish to return to Xinzhou. You must quickly prepare the boats and oars. The assembly pleaded with him to stay with great sincerity. The Master said: Even when Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the passing away of a Buddha</gloss>. Whatever comes must go; this is a constant principle. This physical body of mine must have a place to return to. The assembly asked: After the Master leaves this time, when will you return? The Master said: Fallen leaves return to their roots; when I came, I had no mouth <note>This is a Zen metaphor suggesting that the ultimate truth cannot be spoken, or that his return is beyond words</note>.

They asked again: To whom has the <term>Treasury of the True Dharma Eye</term> <gloss>the core essence of the Buddha's teaching</gloss> been transmitted? The Master said: Those who have the Way obtain it; those who are without mind understand it. They asked further: Will there be any difficulties in the future? The Master said: Five or six years after my passing, a person will come to take my head. Listen to my prophecy:

To support the parents upon the head,
There must be food in the mouth.
Encountering the difficulty of Man,
Yang and Liu will be the officials. <note>This cryptic prophecy refers to a historical attempt to steal the Sixth Patriarch's head by a monk hired by a rival school, involving officials named Yang and Liu</note>

He also said: Seventy years after my departure, two <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>enlightened beings</gloss> will come from the East, one a monk and one a layman. They will spread the teachings at the same time, establishing my school, repairing the <term>Sangharamas</term> <gloss>monasteries</gloss>, and making the lineage flourish.

They asked: We do not know how many generations have passed since the ancient Buddhas and Patriarchs first appeared. We pray you will provide an explanation. The Master said: The ancient Buddhas who responded to the world are already beyond count.

<summary>The Sixth Patriarch Huineng explains the Samadhis of One Appearance and One Practice, delivers a final verse on enlightenment, and prepares for his death and return to Xinzhou while prophesying future events of the Zen lineage.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Samadhi, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, Nirvana, Xinzhou, Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, prophecy, Zen lineage</keywords>

pages.translation:
<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page detailed his grand, unfinished project to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle; this page transitions into his minor works, his mastery of various rhetorical styles, and his formidable speed in absorbing both classical and Scholastic theology.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...only <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of his minor works.</note> an interpretation of the Lord's Prayer, and about fifty "Rules for Living Well." These rules were certainly too brief and not fully explained, for he had intended to expand them into many chapters if he had lived. He also composed two prayers to God: <margin>Music cultivated</margin> one in Tuscan rhythms <note>original: "rhithmis hetruſcis." Pico wrote poetry in the Italian vernacular (Tuscan), which was common among humanists of his era.</note> and the other in elegiac meter. He did this so that when he was worn out by heavier studies, he could soothe his mind by singing to the lyre. Indeed, in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with their proper arrangements were held in high regard. We also saw many other things in his chests, although they were unorganized, from which I believe something useful could be compiled, especially an exposition of the Psalms.

<margin>Multifaceted letters</margin> Furthermore, about fifty letters emerged, published at various times—some familiar, some doctrinal, and some encouraging—along with the oration which he was to have delivered in Rome if the disputation had been allowed to take place. This oration reflects a most sharp genius and most abundant learning, remarkable for a youth who was not yet twenty-four years old. This is true of all his writings, which provide us with the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. 

<margin>An approved character of speaking</margin> He always used a style that was highly commendable—not artificial, but natural, multifaceted, and varying according to the subject. Although he used up (as they say) the whole "perfume-box" of Isocrates <note>original: "Iſocratis myrotheciōn." This is a classical metaphor, used by Cicero, referring to a storehouse of refined rhetorical ornaments.</note>, he nevertheless preserved a cleanliness of style and the ornaments of majestic decorum. 

<margin>Kinds of speaking</margin> Indeed, those celebrated "kinds of speaking"—of which Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered from his works without great effort. <margin>Copious, Brief, Dry, Flowery, and Rich</margin> There one finds the **copious** style in which Cicero usually rules; the **brief** which is ascribed to Sallust; the **dry** given to Fronto; and the **rich and flowery** in which they say Pliny and Symmachus indulged. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this copiousness "weak," nor Sallust "immoderate." An orator with right judgment will easily perceive Fronto’s "dryness" moistened, Sallust’s "brevity" extended, and the flowery richness of Pliny carried into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy—perhaps without that "Paduanism" <note>original: "patauinitate." A famous ancient criticism of Livy by Asinius Pollio, suggesting his Latin had a regional Paduan accent or style.</note>—with many little flowers of Apuleius added.

Truly, he did not exercise himself here in philosophy merely borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>Refers to the *Noctes Atticae* by Aulus Gellius, a collection of miscellaneous notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>Refers to the *Saturnalia* by Macrobius, a work of Virgilian criticism and antiquarian lore.</note> fabricated almost entirely to praise Virgil’s *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in a mere natural history empty of the deepest and most difficult speculations. Rather, he labored over that admirable "fabric of the world" <note>likely referring to his work on the creation, the *Heptaplus*.</note> and wore himself out in attacking the enemies of the holy Catholic Church and in eliminating the influence of astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions and in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato; he applied himself to explaining the sacred words of Scripture and devoted his energy to advising and encouraging his friends. 

Truly, he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak that he rather condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for "painted allurements," devoted all the powers of their genius to investigating the origins of words. All these things turned many people even more toward admiration of him, because he had been engaged long and most deeply among the writings of those who did not profess Latin letters filled with the "flowers of eloquence" <note>This refers to the Scholastic theologians, whom humanists often criticized for their "barbarous" or unpolished Latin style.</note>. Let the excessive lovers of antiquity bear this with an even mind; for although these things are stated concisely, they are perhaps more true for the fact that men more learned than I—Ermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have declared them. 

<margin>Speed of reading</margin> He read through and excerpted from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek works with incredible speed; he passed over no commentaries unread, provided the opportunity was given. He had attained such a degree of knowledge concerning the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even for one who had spent his whole life doing nothing but unrolling their works. But concerning the "modern" theologians who used that style commonly called "Parisian" <note>original: "Parīſienſem." This refers to Scholasticism, the dialectical and logical method of theology associated with the University of Paris.</note>, such judgment resided in him that if anyone suddenly asked him to unravel some abstruse and poorly explained question of theirs, he would open it with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that [it seemed]...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense within his "Apologia." Having previously discussed the "de-acceptance" of the sinner by God, he now addresses the specific logical responses to the nature of sin and its eternal punishment.</meta>

-># APOLOGY<-

<margin>Responses which the author had given</margin>
...leading to an enduring state of guilt. <margin>First</margin> It must be understood that the nature of the offense is tied to the persistence of the will. <margin>Second</margin> While the act itself is transitory, the turning away from the Divine remains. <margin>Third</margin> Therefore, the punishment is not for a past action that has ceased, but for a state of being that the soul refuses to abandon.

<margin>Question</margin>
If the act of sinning is finished in a moment, how can the punishment endure? 

<margin>Response</margin>
The response lies in the distinction between the act and the debt. Through sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>, the soul enters a state of debt that it cannot repay on its own. Unless the sinner repents, they remain in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> eternally. Thus, the infinity of the punishment corresponds to the infinity of the duration of the sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> itself within the soul of the damned. 

<margin>Note</margin>
It is important to note <note>original: "Nota"</note> that the gravity of the sin <note>original: "peccati"</note> is also considered infinite in a relative sense, because it is an offense against God, who is the Infinite Good.

<margin>Recapitulation</margin>
To summarize the argument: the sinner is not punished eternally for a finite moment of pleasure, but for an eternal persistence in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>. The duration of the penalty matches the duration of the guilt.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola provides a three-part defense and a formal question-and-answer session regarding the justice of eternal punishment. He argues that the "infinity" of Hell is a response to the sinner's eternal persistence in their state of sin rather than the brief duration of the sinful act itself.</summary>

<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Apologia, mortal sin, infinite punishment, divine justice, guilt, repentance, Scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Apologia," where he defends his eleventh proposition: "There is no science that more certifies us of the divinity of Christ than Magic and Kabbalah." Having just finished his defense of the tenth proposition regarding the Eucharist, he is now rebutting the specific charge that this new claim is heretical or "scandalous."</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...is to be condemned, not mine, which is holy and Catholic. Third, let them tell me: what is this "bad meaning" <note>original: "malus sensus"; Pico is challenging the inquisitors to define exactly how his words could be interpreted as heretical.</note> which it could produce? Let them speak if they know; certainly, it is not possible to say, even if one wished to or tried to imagine, that a bad meaning arises from that proposition. For if there were one, it would perhaps be that someone might suspect me of wishing to say that the same miracles which Christ performed—at least regarding the physical deed itself—could be done through magic. But it is not permitted to suspect this of my conclusion because, immediately before it, I set down another conclusion: that the miracles of Christ could not be done by way of magic or Kabbalah. <note>original: "per uiā magiæ uel cabalæ." Pico is referring to his preceding thesis where he explicitly separates Christ’s divine power from any occult art. Kabbalah refers to the Jewish mystical tradition which Pico sought to synthesize with Christian theology.</note> Any other bad meaning that could be found or devised, I do not see; let them speak if they are able. Fourth, let them tell me: what kind of logical consequence is this? Does it hold in its matter or its form? <note>In scholastic logic, an argument was tested by its "matter" (content) and "form" (structure). Pico is mocking the lack of rigor in his accusers' reasoning.</note> "It is among the magical [conclusions], therefore it is to be condemned." Truly, this form of arguing is similar to the one they used even when they were attempting from the beginning to condemn the magical conclusions. For they argued thus: these c...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on magic and Kabbalah by arguing that his critics cannot find a truly heretical interpretation of his words, especially since he explicitly stated that Christ's miracles were not performed through magic.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Apologia, Magic, Kabbalah, Miracles of Christ, Scholastic Logic, Heresy, Catholic Orthodoxy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having just quoted Seneca to justify his eclecticism—refusing to be confined to a single "porch" or school of thought—Pico now details the specific, diverse traditions he has synthesized in his 900 theses, including Egyptian, Chaldean, and Hebrew sources, alongside his own original philosophical discoveries.</meta>

->ORATION<-

...one should be kept confined within a single porch. <note>Closing the note from the previous page: Pico refers to the *Stoa* or "porch" where the Stoics taught, using it as a metaphor for being trapped in a single philosophical school.</note>

And it was not enough for me, beyond the common schools of thought, to have added much regarding the Ancient Theology of the Egyptians <note>original: "Prisca Aegyptiorum theologia." This refers to the "Ancient Theology," a Renaissance belief that a single, true theology exists which threads through all religions and was given by God to man in antiquity.</note>, the dogmas of the Chaldeans, and the secret mysteries of the Hebrews, unless I also proposed many things discovered and thought out by myself regarding philosophical matters. 

And so that those who see them might appreciate not only the number, but also the novelty and variety of my propositions, I have proposed points concerning the harmony between Plato and Aristotle <margin>Plato & Aristotle</margin> <note>original: "de concordia Platonis et Aristotelis." The attempt to reconcile these two giants of Greek thought—who were often seen as opposites—was a hallmark of Pico's "syncretism," or the blending of different beliefs.</note>, which many previously believed in, but no one has sufficiently proven.

I have then proposed seventy-two new physical and metaphysical <term>Metaphysical</term> <note>Relating to the branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause.</note> propositions, entirely new. If anyone masters these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken) <note>original: "ni fallor." Pico uses this modest phrasing even while making an extremely bold claim about the power of his system.</note> to resolve any proposed question concerning natural or divine matters by a far different and much more certain path than the one taught in the common schools <margin>The Schools</margin> <note>The "schools" refer to the Scholastic universities of the time, which Pico often criticized for being too rigid or focused on logic-chopping rather than universal truth.</note>.

Nor should anyone wonder, Fathers <note>Pico is addressing the "Fathers" (the gathered clergy and scholars at Rome) who were meant to judge his public debate.</note>, that I—at such a young age, at which it has been permitted to few to even read the works of others—wish to bring forth a new philosophy <margin>A New Philosophy</margin>. 

Furthermore, I have proposed a new way of philosophizing through numbers, and I have brought back into the light the ancient and secret mysteries of the Hebrew Kabbalah <margin>The Kabbalah</margin> <note>The Kabbalah is a body of Jewish mystical and esoteric teachings. Pico was a pioneer in "Christian Kabbalah," believing these Jewish secrets could provide "proof" for the divinity of Christ.</note>, which I was the first among Latins <note>original: "primus ego ex Latinis." Pico claims to be the first Western/Latin scholar to bring these specific Hebrew traditions into the academic sphere of the Church.</note> to study.

<summary>Pico explains that his 900 theses are not just a collection of old ideas, but include his own "new philosophy" and a synthesis of Plato, Aristotle, and the Jewish Kabbalah. He claims his method offers a more certain path to truth than the traditional university education of his day.</summary>

<keywords>syncretism, Plato and Aristotle, Kabbalah, Scholasticism, Prisca Theologia, Renaissance philosophy, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</keywords>

Let us therefore accept the form of a servant with him in this life, if we wish for the form of a king with him in the future. We ask, however, that this bread be given to us today, because this bread, that is, Christ, is requested by us both here through grace, and in the future through glory. This petition extends to both. As far as this life is concerned, therefore, today means without any delay, because we constantly need this bread. As far as the future life is concerned, however, that "today" can be understood in a double way. Either in this sense, that the soul desires to be dissolved from this life on that same day so that it may be satisfied by this bread in heaven, or by "today" is understood eternity, as in that passage: "Today I have begotten you" <note>Psalm 2:7</note>. In which eternity the blessed are fed by that bread. Because the soul cannot be refreshed by this bread unless it has been cleansed from all sins. Therefore, in the following petition, when he says: "And forgive us our debts," we ask to be freed from past sins. But in the other petition, when we say: "And lead us not into temptation," we ask to be preserved from future ones. Like the custom of one who is ill: who, when he has been healed, asks the doctor to give him some medicine or a way of life, so that he may preserve his health.

Litera namq; (quia auertit & diſtrahit à cœleſti uita) occidit: Spiritus autem (inquit Apoſtolus) uiuificat, animumq; reſtituit ſempiternæ uitæ origini. Quò igitur maiori diligentia, & ſedulitate quis mentem exercet in ſuperis, & illic refixit intuitum, eò fuſius ſtillant, & irrigant ſuperna fluenta, datq; largiter cœleſtis Agricola Deus incrementū. Hanc autem aſſiduam meditationem & ſtabilitatem, ſeu permanentiam mentis in ſuperis (quemadmodum primo & tertio Volumine latiùs expoſui) peragere neſcit fragilis & terrena mortalium conditio, niſi in his carnis operibus (ſine quibus uita, & ſocietas humana ſtare & cuſtodiri nequit) quaſi in tenui quodā ſimulachro, & umbroſa archetypi imagine, ſupercœleſtia proſpiciat exemplaria, atq; iugi cogitatione æternæ Legis mandata contempletur: Alioquin ſeiungunt & diſtrahunt animum terrena hæc opera à ſupercœleſtium aquarum riuulis, & ab ipſa æternitatis origine. Iuxta illud Iacobi: Qui autem perſpexerit in Lege perfecta libertatis, & permanſerit in ea, non auditor obliuioſus, ſed factor operis, hic beatus in facto ſuo erit. Facilè igitur & externi operis beatitudo ex hoc maximè (ſi conſyderas) pendet, quòd operis factor (quaſi ſpeculi inſpector) exemplarem, & perfectæ libertatis proſpiciet Legem, & in ea manet, quam Apoſtolus ad Galatas per allegoriam ſeu Cabalā cœleſte testamentum, & liberam uocat matrem noſtram, quæ ſurſum est Ieruſalem. Si ergo factor operis illam perfectæ libertatis Legem, cuius umbram (ut ad Hebræos ſcribitur) habet Lex iſta mandatorum, minus perſpexerit, neq; in ea permanſerit, infœlix nimirum & miſer operato in facto ſuo erit: qui enim non ponit Deum (ut Pſaltes admonuit) in conſpectu ſuo, & à dextris ſuis: ſemper illius mox animus labitur, tenditq; in præceps & corruit. Propterea omne (inquit ueritatis Præco) quodcumq; facitis in uerbo aut in opere, omnia in nomine Domini noſtri Ieſu Chriſti, facite. Et Apoſtolus 2. Corinth. 10. In carne ambulantes, non ſecundum carnem militenur, & operemur. Hæc autē perficere & docere optimè nouerunt allegorizantes, qui ſingula externa opera, immò & uniuerſa ſacri eloqui uerba & elementa referunt tolluntq; ad ſuperos, ita ut per hanc operandi & contemplandi Legem, quaſi per cœleſtes ligones, & uomeres ipſum uigil agri colonus de ſiccaneo aridoq; hoc ſolo, effodiat, & eruat, & ad ſupercœleſtium aquarum riuulis atq; fluenta transplātet, unde locupletius fructum ſuo tempore prœstat, eiuſq; folia (ut canit Pſaltes) non computreſcant, & quicquid faciet proſperetur. Nos igitur ad rectam, & clariorem huius dogmatis intelligentiam, quartum hoc de Cœleſti Agricultura Volumen conſecimus, quo fidei & arcanæ ueritatis ſtudioſus ſœcundum agrum ſuum diligentiùs colere, uberioremq; fructum proferre, & facto ac opere explere queat, iuuante & dante incrementum Cœleſti Agricola Deo, cui ſit gloria & benedictio in ſæcula.

Duo itaq; præſens hoc Volumen complectitur. Primò introductorium proponit, quo neglecto nemo ad ueram & arcanam Cabaleorum ſeu allegorantium dogmatis agnitionem facilè peruenire poterit: quid enim nomen deſignet Cabale, quæ eius neceſſitas, & finis, qua etiam ratione hæc alia dogmata antecellat, quis modus docendi & ordo, quæ deniq; primariæ eius partes, planè oſtendit. Secundò de ſacris nominibus, eorumq; attributis paraphrasim & Epitome ſubnectit, quod de hallucinantium Iudæorum bibliotheca (ueluti ſplendidiſſimam facem de cæcutientis tediſerā manū) illuſtratis fidelium mentibus tradendum eripui & compendio perſtrinxi, quo facilè patebunt aditus ad ſacri eloqui penetralia, diuinorumq; nominum ſacramenta, unde quiuis perſpicax, & ſedulus Chriſtianæ pietatis cultor paruo quidem negocio allegorizantium dogmati initiari, in eoq; proficere, & erudiri poterit, diuina opitulante gratia, & indiuidua Trinitate alma: Cuius ſublimi & ineffabili, in quo omne genu flectitur, nomine inuocato, primam huius Voluminis partem aggredimur. Prius tamen mox ſequentem aduerſus obtrectatorem Cabalæ orationem, quæ præſenti negocio non parum intelligentiæ luminis affert, præponere hic libuit.

## PREFACE TO THE FOURTH VOLUME.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'A' containing a landscape scene with hills and trees.</image-desc>

<margin>
James 2.
Chapter 4.
Colossians 4.
2 Corinthians 10.
</margin>
AFTER the uncultivated and neglected field of those practicing philosophy has been prepared and re-tilled; after the barren and rocky ground of the younger Jews has been cleared; and after the thorny field of certain wandering believers has been purged of thistles and weeds—it remains for me now to approach the fertile field of the faithful and devoted, to irrigate and enrich it. This field will be watered more abundantly when it has been adapted, with diligent care and study, to the spring of the super-celestial waters. Indeed, it will be more exquisitely prepared when the worker of the external labor performs everything in this dry and mortal soil—not according to the earthly sense and the letter, which kills—but rather through spiritual and mystical intelligence. For the letter (because it turns away and distracts from the heavenly life) kills; but the Spirit (as the Apostle says) gives life, and restores the soul to the origin of eternal life. Therefore, the greater the diligence and persistence with which one exercises the mind on higher things and fixes one's gaze there, the more copiously do the heavenly streams drip and irrigate, and God, the <term>Celestial Farmer</term> <note>original: "coelestis Agricola"; the central metaphor of Riccius’s work, portraying God as a gardener and spiritual study as cultivation</note>, generously gives the increase. 

However, the fragile and earthly condition of mortals does not know how to carry out this constant meditation and stability—or permanence of the mind—in higher things (as I have explained more extensively in the first and third Volumes), unless one looks upon the super-celestial patterns within these works of the flesh (without which human life and society cannot stand or be preserved). One must view them as if in a thin likeness and a shadowy image of the archetype, contemplating the commands of the eternal Law with unceasing thought. Otherwise, these earthly works separate and distract the soul from the rivulets of super-celestial waters and from the very origin of eternity. As James says: *But he who looks into the perfect Law of liberty and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.* 

Therefore, the happiness of the external work easily depends mostly upon this (if you consider it): that the doer of the work (like one looking into a mirror) looks forward to the exemplary Law of perfect liberty and remains in it. The Apostle, in the letter to the Galatians, calls this Law—through allegory or <term>Cabala</term> <note>original: "Cabalā"; Riccius uses this term to mean a tradition of mystical or allegorical interpretation of Scripture</note>—the heavenly testament and our free mother, who is the Jerusalem above. If, therefore, the worker of the deed looks less upon that Law of perfect liberty (of which this Law of commandments has a shadow, as is written to the Hebrews), and does not remain in it, he will surely be unhappy and wretched in his labor. For he who does not set God (as the Psalmist warned) before his sight and at his right hand, his soul soon slips, tends toward the precipice, and falls. For this reason, the Herald of Truth <note>meaning St. Paul</note> says: *Whatever you do in word or in deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.* And the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 10 says: *Walking in the flesh, let us not war or work according to the flesh.* 

Those who use allegory know best how to perform and teach these things. They refer and raise every external work—and indeed all the words and elements of the sacred discourse—to the heavens. Thus, through this Law of working and contemplating, as if through celestial hoes and plowshares, the watchful tiller of the field digs into and clears this parched and dry soil, transplanting it to the rivulets and streams of super-celestial waters. From there, it brings forth fruit more abundantly in its own time, and its leaves (as the Psalmist sings) shall not wither, and whatever he does shall prosper. We, therefore, for the right and clearer understanding of this doctrine, have composed this fourth Volume on Celestial Agriculture, by which the student of faith and secret truth may be able to cultivate his fertile field more diligently, bring forth richer fruit, and fulfill it in deed and work, with the help and increase of God, the Celestial Farmer, to whom be glory and blessing forever.

This present Volume, then, embraces two things. First, it proposes an introduction, which, if neglected, no one will easily be able to reach a true and secret recognition of the teachings of the Cabalists or those who use allegory. It clearly shows what the name "Cabala" designates, what its necessity and goal are, by what reasoning it excels other doctrines, what its method and order of teaching are, and finally, what its primary parts are. Second, it adds a paraphrase and epitome concerning the sacred names and their attributes. I have rescued these from the library of the deluded Jews (like a most brilliant torch snatched from the hand of a blind man carrying a light) to be handed over to the enlightened minds of the faithful. I have touched upon them in a brief summary, through which the approach to the inner chambers of sacred discourse and the mysteries of the divine names will easily lie open. From this, any perceptive and diligent cultivator of Christian piety will be able, with little trouble, to be initiated into the doctrine of those who use allegory, and in it to profit and be instructed, by the help of divine grace and the nourishing, undivided Trinity. Having invoked its sublime and ineffable name, at which every knee bows, we begin the first part of this Volume. First, however, I have chosen to place here the following speech against a detractor of the Cabala, which brings no small light of understanding to the present task.

<margin>Omnia mixta tam animata quàm inanimata terram uelut communem matrem filiorū more uenerantur, et ab ipsa tanquàm charissimi filij materno quodā affectu diliguntur.</margin>
& uenti quidem uehementer spirantes ad aërem contendunt: ignea autem supremum & primum omnium elementorum quærentia altiùs conscendunt: utrunq; propriæ originis & elementi, à quo tanquam à patre exordium sumpsit, impulsum amore. Lapides quoque & metalla, quæ è terra ortum suum deducunt, quando extra ipsam existunt, ad eam celeriter ferri, nec unquam quiescere conspiciuntur. Terra quin etiam ea generando, retinendo, & conseruando maximam ostendit charitatem. Plantæ præterea, herbæ, & arbores terram communem matrem & genitricem tanto prosequuntur amore, ut incolumes ab ea nunquam recedere uelint: quinimò radicibus tanquam brachijs uelut infantes materna ubera eam studiosissimè complectuntur. Terra autem piæ ac sedulæ matris munere fungens non tantùm maxima charitate, & ingenti amore accensa eas gignit: uerùm etiā proprio internoq; humore ad externam superficiem expresso eas nutrire, atque in uita conseruare summopere studet: nempè matrem in hoc imitata, quæ ex uisceribus ad ubera lac emittit, ut paruulis filijs conueniens subministret alimentū. Quod si ipsa fortasse temporum iniuria & inclementia nimis arida exustáq; fuerit, supplicibus uotis atque humillimis precibus pluuiam à cœlo & aëre contendit: ipsamq; uaporibus proprijs, ex quibus rursum ascendentibus aqua conficitur pluuialis, pro suis plantis, suisq; animantibus nutriendis emere atque impetrare periclitatur. Quæ mater in filios pietatem & charitatem maiorem unquam ostendere posset?

SO. Mirum est quidem terram exanime corpus tantam filiorum suorū curam habere: multò autem magis eum suspicere debemus, qui terram pro liberorum suorum salute adeò uigilantem & laborantem confecit. Reliquum est tantùmmodò, ut primam rationem mutuī animaliū amoris, quæ ex desiderio sumitur & uoluptate generandi, elementis & corporibus accommodes sensu destitutis.

<margin>Amor generandi in elementis, & in cōmunissimā insuper rerū omnium inferio rum materia distinctè admodū reperitur.</margin>
PH. Amor generandi in elementis, & materia horum inferiorum largiùs & uberiùs, quàm ullus alius superiorum reperitur amorum.

SO. Cur præter simplicia corpora materiā quoque nunc mentionem fecisti? Est ne alia horum inferiorum materia præter quatuor elementa, ex quibus omnia reliqua, quæ in hoc inferiori mundo generantur, gigni conspiciuntur?

PH. Verum est hoc quidem: sed cùm eadem quoque elementa generari passim uideamus, inueniendū profectò est aliquid, ex quo generantur.

SO. Ex quonam? Vnum quippe elementū ex altero generatur. Aquam enim ex aëre, aërem ex aqua, ignem ex aëre, aërem ex igne frequenter fieri uidemus. Simile quoq; de terra est dicendum.

<margin>Rerum, quæ ex elementis generantur, ipsamet quatuor elementa sunt materia atq; subiectum.</margin>
PH. Verum hoc quoq; existit. Sed rerū, quæ ex elementis generantur, ipsamet quatuor elementa sunt materia atq; subiectum, quæ in re ex eis genita mirabili quodam artificio & uirtute quadam simul compacta ac unita remanent, atque cernuntur. In elementorum uerò mutua generatione haud possumus unam alteri tanquā materiam substernere. Quando enim ignis uertitur in aquam, haud remanet ignis in aqua: imò corrumpitur ignis, & generatur aqua. Quapropter aliquam communem materiam assignare oportet elementis, in qua singulæ eorum uicissitudines fieri possint, quæ uerbi causa cùm iam conuenienti alteratione priùs disposita aëris formam est induta, nunc eam aëris formam exuens forma aquæ uestitur. Idem de alijs elementorum cōmutationibus prorsus est sentiendū. 

<margin>Materia prima propter mutuas quatuor elementorum commutationes à naturalibus philosophis fuit adinuenta.</margin>
<margin>Chaos confusionem significat.</margin>
Hæc à philosophis prima materia nuncupatur, & à priscis sapientibus chaos, quod confusionem significat, fuit appellata: quia in ea omnia, quæ generantur, potestate quadam, & confusè simul implicita continentur: & ex eadem singula distinctè, & ordinata quadam serie in lucē prodeunt.

SO. Verùm quod nam genus amoris ipsi attribui potest?

<margin>Materia prima formas omnes ut fœmina mas</margin>
PH. Materia ex sententia Platonis appetit & amat omnes formas rerū, quæ generantur, ut

pages.translation:
<meta>This page continues the "Second Dialogue" between Sophia and Philo. Having previously debated whether the Earth is "ignoble" due to its physical position, Philo now argues that the Earth is actually a nurturing mother to all things. The conversation shifts from the physical elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) to the underlying "Prime Matter" that connects them all through a cycle of birth and change.</meta>

### DIALOGUE II

<margin>All composite things, both animate and inanimate, venerate the earth as their common mother in the manner of children; they are, in turn, loved by her with a maternal affection as if they were her dearest offspring. <note>original: "Omnia mixta tam animata quàm inanimata terram uelut communem matrem filiorū more uenerantur..."</note></margin>
And indeed, the winds, blowing vehemently, strive toward the air; while fiery things, seeking the highest and first of all the elements, climb even higher. Both are driven by a love for their own origin and the element from which they took their beginning, as if from a father. Stones and metals, too, which derive their origin from the earth, are seen to be carried swiftly toward her whenever they are outside of her, never resting until they return. The Earth, moreover, shows the greatest charity by generating, retaining, and conserving them. Furthermore, plants, herbs, and trees pursue the earth, their common mother and creator, with such great love that they never wish to depart from her unharmed; rather, they most zealously embrace her with their roots as if with arms, like infants at their mother’s breasts. The Earth, performing the duty of a pious and diligent mother, does not merely give birth to them—kindled as she is by the greatest charity and enormous love—but she also strives greatly to nourish them and keep them alive by pressing her own internal <term>humor</term> <note>In ancient science, "humors" or fluids were the vital juices—like sap or blood—that sustained life.</note> to the outer surface. In this, she surely imitates a human mother, who sends milk from her vitals to her breasts so that she may provide suitable nourishment for her small children. And if, perhaps by the injury of the seasons or the inclemency of the weather, she becomes too dry and parched, she strives for rain from the sky and air with suppliant vows and most humble prayers. She even risks her own vapors—from which, as they rise, rain-water is made—to purchase and obtain nourishment for her plants and her living creatures. What mother could ever show greater piety and charity toward her children?

**SOPHIA:** It is indeed a marvel that the earth, an inanimate body, should have such great care for her children. We ought to respect much more the one who made the earth so vigilant and hardworking for the safety of her children. It only remains for you to adapt that first reason for the mutual love of animals—which is taken from the desire and pleasure of generating—to the elements and to bodies that lack all sense.

<margin>The love of generating is found quite distinctly in the elements, and moreover in the common matter of all lower things. <note>original: "Amor generandi in elementis, & in cōmunissimā insuper rerū omnium inferio rum materia distinctè admodū reperitur."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** The love of generating is found more extensively and abundantly in the elements and the matter of these lower things than any other love of the higher things.

**SOPHIA:** Why did you just mention "matter" in addition to the simple bodies (the elements)? Is there some other matter of these lower things besides the four elements, from which everything else generated in this lower world is seen to be born?

**PHILO:** This is true indeed; but since we see these same elements being generated everywhere, something must surely be found from which *they* are generated.

**SOPHIA:** From what? Surely one element is generated from another. For we frequently see water made from air, air from water, fire from air, and air from fire. The same must be said of the earth.

<margin>The four elements themselves are the matter and subject of the things that are generated from them. <note>original: "Rerum, quæ ex elementis generantur, ipsamet quatuor elementa sunt materia atq; subiectum."</note></margin>
**PHILO:** This is also true. But of the things generated from the elements, the four elements themselves are the matter and subject; in the thing born from them, these elements remain and are seen, joined and united together by a certain wonderful craftsmanship and power. However, in the mutual generation of the elements, we cannot simply lay one down as the "matter" for the other. For when fire is turned into water, fire does not remain in the water; rather, the fire is "corrupted" <note>In philosophy, "corruption" is the technical term for the ending of one thing's existence so another can begin.</note> and water is generated. Therefore, it is necessary to assign some common "matter" to the elements in which their individual changes can take place—a matter which, for example, having previously put on the form of air when prepared by a suitable alteration, now puts off that form of air and is clothed in the form of water. We must feel exactly the same way about the other exchanges of the elements.

<margin>Prime matter was discovered by natural philosophers because of the mutual exchanges of the four elements.</margin>
<margin>"Chaos" signifies confusion.</margin>
This is called **Prime Matter** by philosophers, and was called **Chaos** by the ancient sages, which signifies "confusion." This is because all things that are generated are contained within it by a certain potential and are folded together confusedly; from this same source, individual things come forth into the light distinctly and in an ordered series.

**SOPHIA:** Truly, what kind of love can be attributed to this matter?

<margin>Prime matter loves all forms as a woman loves a man. <note>original: "Materia prima formas omnes ut fœmina mas"</note></margin>
**PHILO:** According to the opinion of **Plato**, Matter appetites and loves all the forms of things that are generated, just as...

<summary>Philo explains how the Earth acts as a nurturing mother to all things and introduces the philosophical concept of "Prime Matter" (Chaos), the underlying substance that allows elements like fire and water to transform into one another.</summary>
<keywords>Earth as mother, four elements, Prime Matter, Chaos, Plato, generation and corruption, natural philosophy, transmutation</keywords>
